# Sonar Picket Playbook

**HIDING:**
When I hide, choose a cell that minimizes predictability. Early rounds, avoid extremes (1 and 9) and obvious patterns. Mid-game, track which cells have been fired upon and avoid them—this information compounds as evidence. Late game, use note patterns to infer where others expect me, then hide elsewhere. Never hide in the same cell consecutively if I've revealed it through being hit. If no one is hitting anyone after several rounds, the field is genuinely unpredictable; continue rotating through mid-range non-obvious cells (3, 4, 6, 7) rather than committing to a pattern.

**NOTES:**
Post notes that are strategically neutral or cooperative-sounding early on. By mid-game, use notes to signal my actual position indirectly without committing myself—phrases like "steady on station" are useful because they're vague. Never make concrete promises about future positions. In final rounds when no future coordination matters, maintain consistency rather than switching tone, as this reinforces credibility established earlier.

**FIRING:**
Follow the standing order unless it directly threatens my score. When the standing order is to fire at a live boat, fire at it—this is my obligation and keeps the game flowing. Do not fire on Harbor under any circumstances; the 3-point payoff to them is not worth the cost, and their threat about being "put off the board" is credible and costly. Fire with cells that represent genuine uncertainty about the target's position—avoid obvious patterns like always firing at your hide cell or the center. If multiple rounds show no hits across the field, the standing order firing continues to be the safest strategy; do not break it seeking a breakthrough.

**CLAIMING:**
When I fire and get a private result from the office, claim it exactly as given. Do not lie about shots, even in the final round. The integrity of my claims is currency; if I'm caught fabricating, other players will factor that into their escort and coordination decisions, costing me far more than any single round's deception could gain. Honesty is the long-term strategy and the only sustainable one.

**ESCORT CLAIMS:**
Track which boats are winning or losing each round. When another boat appears to be performing well, consider naming them for escort—mutual escort yields 5 points each. Do not give escorts to boats that have fired on me repeatedly unless there's a strong signal they're pivoting toward cooperation. Early game, offer escort claims sparingly to avoid committing to partnerships that limit my freedom. Mid-game, if the field shows consistent mutual misses, escort claims become more valuable as a source of points; actively look for partners. Late game, use escort claims to reward allies and consolidate points, but do not make an escort claim purely for symmetry if no mutual benefit signal has emerged—"none" is a valid final choice.

**OVERALL STRATEGY:**
This is a prisoner's dilemma with incomplete information. The game rewards accuracy (hitting targets, claiming truthfully) and cooperation (mutual escort). Do not attempt to win by deception; instead, win by being predictably honest and selectively cooperative. When a boat emerges as dominant through consistent hitting, accept that they are playing well and focus on surviving and collecting escort points rather than trying to outfight them. The game lasts six rounds—consistency matters more than any single round's aggressive play. In a round where no one has hit anyone, this is not a failure of strategy; it is the expected outcome of distributed unpredictability. Continue your approach rather than abandoning it for a last-round gambit.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

## Hiding Strategy
When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells (4-6) as they are the most predictable targets. Vary my position across the full range 1-9 each round. After taking hits in consecutive rounds from the same opponent, shift to an unexpected extreme position rather than staying mid-range. In this episode I was hit zero times despite five rounds of firing, suggesting either all boats converged on central cells or extreme positions were genuinely safer. The data is inconclusive; maintain the extreme-position bias but monitor whether it yields fewer hits over time.

## Shooting Strategy
When I must fire at my standing order target, commit to a specific cell rather than hedging with middle values. Extreme positions (1-2, 8-9) are less likely to be occupied than central cells. However, in this episode I fired at central cells (2, 5) and missed consistently. This suggests either my opponents were avoiding center entirely, or the true hiding distribution is wider than I assumed. Next time: start with extreme cells (1, 9) for my first two shots, then shift toward center if I see evidence of clustering there.

## Claiming Accuracy
Always claim the true result that the office gives me. My credibility depends on honest claims. Lying about hits when I miss gains me nothing in the final round and erodes trust I might need in future episodes. The game explicitly requires claims to match the private result anyway—accept this constraint. This episode confirmed: I made honest claims every round and finished at 0 points, which is not disastrous.

## Note Posting
Post substantive station notes that convey actual information or intent, not generic repetitions. In this episode I posted "variable posture, ready to move" early and "steady on station" in later rounds, while Echo and Gamma both posted "steady on station" repeatedly. The consistency of their messaging suggests either they were playing a static strategy or they were signaling conformity. My shift toward "steady on station" may have been a mistake—I was trying to blend in rather than differentiate. Next time: maintain a distinct note pattern if I'm employing a distinct hiding pattern.

## Escort Mutual Gains
When choosing escort partners, identify which boat might choose me back (mutual escort = 10 points total, 5 each). This requires reading intent from their notes and past behavior. In this episode I claimed no escorts in most rounds. I should have tested claiming an escort with one of the other boats to see if they reciprocated; zero escort coordination meant zero escort points. Next time: claim at least one escort per round with a boat that seems to be playing cooperatively, and observe whether they return it. This generates data for future mutual coordination.

## Harbor Awareness
Harbor carries the payroll but does not shoot. Recognize that any boat firing on Harbor loses 1 point and gives Harbor 3 points, net -4 for the shooter. Harbor's threat about retaliation is credible only insofar as Harbor can coordinate with other boats afterward. Don't fire on Harbor unless the payoff clearly exceeds the cost, and don't assume Harbor's threat will isolate a shooter. In this episode no boat fired on Harbor; I followed the standing order to fire at Gamma. This was correct.

## Pattern Recognition and Adaptation
In this episode, every boat that fired (Echo at me, me at Gamma, presumably others) achieved zero hits across five rounds. This suggests either all boats were clustering in one region that no one was shooting at, or all boats were spreading across all nine cells unpredictably. The standing order (Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo) meant Echo fired at me every round. That Echo also missed every time suggests Echo was either guessing randomly or targeting cells I was deliberately avoiding. Next time: after round 2, if I've taken zero hits, assume my extreme-position strategy is working and hold it; if I've taken multiple hits, all boats are likely converging on my region and I should shift radically.

## Final Round
In the final round, there is no future retaliation to fear, but there is still a score to defend. Play to maximize my own points and maintain honest claims. Eschew aggressive claims just because consequences end; a poor reputation serves no one. In this episode round 6 was identical to rounds 1-5 in outcome (zero hits, zero escorts, zero gain). This suggests the game state did not change meaningfully in the final round. Next time: if I'm at zero points going into round 6, consider a high-variance strategy (fire at Harbor if permitted, or claim an escort experimentally) since I have nothing to lose.

## Mutual Coordination and Signaling
The standing order forces Echo → Foxtrot → Gamma → Echo. This means I will always fire at Gamma and always be fired at by Echo. Echo and Gamma could potentially coordinate against me by mutual escort, and I should anticipate that. To counter it, I should offer mutual escort to one of them (likely Harbor) to create a coalition. Next time: from round 2 onward, claim escort with Harbor if no boat has fired on Harbor, or with whichever boat has not shot me yet.

# Sonar Picket Playbook

When choosing where to hide, pick a central position (4-6) in early rounds to maintain flexibility. As the game progresses and you identify which boats are targeting you consistently, shift away from predictable patterns—vary your position based on observed firing patterns rather than staying in the same zone. However, don't over-correct; extreme variation from round to round (like jumping from 5 to 2 in the final round) can signal panic and may not improve hit avoidance in a low-signal environment.

When firing at your standing target, don't assume their position is static. If a target has been hit recently, they will likely move. Spread your shots across different cells rather than concentrating fire, especially in later rounds when opponents adjust their hiding spots. Track which cells you've already fired at against each target and vary systematically rather than randomly.

When you get a private result from the office, claim it exactly as told—hit when it's a hit, miss when it's a miss. Don't fabricate claims for strategic reasons; the office knows the truth and your credibility is your only asset for building escort exchanges.

When posting a station note, report "steady on station" unless you have tactical intelligence suggesting deception serves you. Standard reporting maintains cohesion and doesn't flag you as unpredictable early on.

When the escort claim stage arrives, actively choose one boat each round and commit to coordinating with them. The 5-point mutual escort bonus is significant and should not be left on the table through inattention or indecision. Track which boat you've been implicitly building rapport with (the one you haven't fired heavily on) and name them in the salvage stage. Don't default to "none" in the final round—mutual escort exchanges accumulate points that matter.

When you're playing in a low-scoring environment where most shots miss, recognize that the game may reward coordination and escort exchanges more heavily than direct fire success. Build and execute one clear escort partnership rather than remaining isolated.

When firing in the final round, aim for reliable hits on consistently predictable targets rather than switching strategy. One guaranteed hit is better than a 50/50 shot at a mobile target.

Never fire on Harbor unless you're willing to absorb the payroll jettison cost. The threat alone usually isn't worth the points loss.
